facts.title: The symbol Au
facts.statement: Gold has the chemical symbol Au, from the Latin aurum, meaning 'shining dawn'.
facts.question: Which element has the chemical symbol Au?
facts.hook: Odd symbols like Au, Ag, Fe and Pb all come from Latin names, not English ones.

facts.title: The symbol Ag
facts.statement: Silver has the chemical symbol Ag, from the Latin argentum. Argentina is named after it.
facts.question: Which element has the chemical symbol Ag?
facts.details:
Silver is a chemical element; it has symbol Ag (from Latin  argentum 'silver') and atomic number 47. A soft, white, lustrous transition metal, it exhibits the highest electrical conductivity, thermal conductivity and reflectivity of any metal. Silver is found in the Earth's crust in the pure, free elemental form ("native silver"), as an alloy with gold and other metals, and in minerals such as acanthite, argentite and chlorargyrite. Most silver is recovered as a byproduct of lead–zinc, copper and gold mining and refining.
Silver has long been valued as a precious metal and coinage metal. It is one of the seven metals of antiquity, and has had an enduring role in monetary systems, jewellery, tableware and decorative arts. Its purity is commonly measured on a per-mille basis; a 94%-pure alloy is described as "0.940 fine". Because pure silver is relatively soft, silver used in jewellery, coinage and household objects is often alloyed with copper or other metals.
Beyond currency and investment uses such as coins and bullion, silver is an important industrial material. It is used in photovoltaics, electrical contacts and conductors, printed electronics, brazing alloys, catalysis, specialised mirrors and window coatings, and antimicrobial materials.

facts.title: The symbol Fe
facts.statement: Iron has the chemical symbol Fe, from the Latin ferrum, and makes up most of the Earth's core.
facts.question: Which element has the chemical symbol Fe?

facts.title: The symbol Pb
facts.statement: Lead has the chemical symbol Pb, from the Latin plumbum — the same root as 'plumbing', because Roman pipes were made of it.
facts.question: Which element has the chemical symbol Pb?
facts.hook: Plumbum gave us both 'Pb' and 'plumber'.
facts.details:
Lead ( ) is a chemical element with the symbol Pb (from the Latin plumbum) and atomic number 82. It is a heavy metal, denser than most common materials. Lead is soft, malleable, and has a relatively low melting point. When freshly cut or melted, it appears shiny silvery with a bluish tint, but tarnishes to dull gray on exposure to air. Lead has the highest atomic number of any stable element, and three of its isotopes are endpoints of major nuclear decay chains of heavier elements.
Lead is a relatively un-reactive post-transition metal. Its weak metallic character is shown by its amphoteric behavior: lead and lead oxides react with both acids and bases, and it tends to form covalent bonds. Lead compounds usually occur in the +2 oxidation state rather than the +4 state common in lighter members of the carbon group, with exceptions mostly limited to organolead compounds. Like the lighter members of the group, lead can bond with itself, forming chains and polyhedral structures.
Since lead is easily extracted from its ores, prehistoric people in the Near East were aware of it.

facts.title: The symbol Na
facts.statement: Sodium has the chemical symbol Na, from the Latin natrium. It is so reactive it is stored under oil.
facts.question: Which element has the chemical symbol Na?

facts.title: The symbol K
facts.statement: Potassium has the chemical symbol K, from the Latin kalium. It is essential for nerve and muscle function.
facts.question: Which element has the chemical symbol K?

facts.title: The symbol Hg
facts.statement: Mercury has the chemical symbol Hg, from hydrargyrum meaning 'water-silver'. It is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature.
facts.question: Which element has the chemical symbol Hg?

facts.title: The highest melting point
facts.statement: Tungsten has the highest melting point of any metal, 3,422°C, which is why it was used for light-bulb filaments.
facts.question: Which metal has the highest melting point?

facts.title: Most abundant element in the universe
facts.statement: Hydrogen is the most abundant element in the universe, making up about 75% of all normal matter.
facts.question: What is the most abundant element in the universe?

facts.title: Most abundant element in the Earth's crust
facts.statement: Oxygen is the most abundant element in the Earth's crust by mass — about 46% — mostly locked up in silicate rocks.
facts.question: What is the most abundant element in the Earth's crust?
facts.hook: Most of the planet's oxygen is in rock, not air.

facts.title: The main gas in air
facts.statement: Nitrogen makes up about 78% of the Earth's atmosphere — far more than oxygen's 21%.
facts.question: Which gas makes up most of the Earth's atmosphere?
facts.hook: Air is mostly the gas you do not breathe for.

facts.title: The second-lightest element
facts.statement: Helium is the second-lightest and second most abundant element, and the only one first discovered in space — in the Sun's spectrum — before being found on Earth.
facts.question: Which element was first discovered in the Sun before being found on Earth?
facts.hook: Named after Helios, the Greek sun god.

facts.title: The element of life
facts.statement: Carbon forms the backbone of all known life because it can form four stable bonds, building chains and rings of almost unlimited complexity.
facts.question: Which element forms the chemical backbone of all known life?

facts.title: Largest planet
facts.statement: Jupiter is the largest planet in the Solar System — more massive than all the others combined — and its Great Red Spot is a storm that has raged for centuries.
facts.question: What is the largest planet in the Solar System?

facts.title: Hottest planet
facts.statement: Venus is the hottest planet, at about 465°C, because a runaway carbon dioxide greenhouse traps heat — even though Mercury is closer to the Sun.
facts.question: Which is the hottest planet in the Solar System?
facts.hook: Closest to the Sun does not mean hottest — the atmosphere decides.

facts.title: The red planet
facts.statement: Mars looks red because its surface is covered in iron oxide — rust. It hosts Olympus Mons, the tallest volcano in the Solar System.
facts.question: Which planet is known as the Red Planet?

facts.title: The ringed planet
facts.statement: Saturn's rings are made mostly of water ice and are only tens of metres thick despite spanning hundreds of thousands of kilometres.
facts.question: Which planet is famous for its extensive ring system?

facts.title: Closest planet to the Sun
facts.statement: Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun and the smallest in the Solar System, with a year lasting just 88 Earth days.
facts.question: Which planet is closest to the Sun?

facts.title: The farthest planet
facts.statement: Neptune is the farthest planet from the Sun and has the fastest winds in the Solar System, over 2,000 km/h.
facts.question: Which is the farthest planet from the Sun?
facts.hook: Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006.

facts.title: The planet on its side
facts.statement: Uranus rotates on its side, tilted about 98 degrees, probably after an ancient collision — so its poles take turns facing the Sun for 42 years each.
facts.question: Which planet rotates on its side, tilted about 98 degrees?

facts.title: The densest planet
facts.statement: Earth is the densest planet in the Solar System, thanks to its large iron core.
facts.question: Which is the densest planet in the Solar System?

facts.title: Theory of relativity
facts.statement: Albert Einstein published special relativity in 1905 and general relativity in 1915, redefining gravity as the curvature of spacetime.
facts.question: Who developed the theory of relativity?

facts.title: Laws of motion and gravitation
facts.statement: Isaac Newton formulated the three laws of motion and universal gravitation, and co-invented calculus.
facts.question: Who formulated the three laws of motion?

facts.title: Evolution by natural selection
facts.statement: Charles Darwin published On the Origin of Species in 1859, explaining how species change through natural selection.
facts.question: Who proposed the theory of evolution by natural selection?

facts.title: Two Nobel Prizes in two sciences
facts.statement: Marie Curie discovered polonium and radium, and remains the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences — Physics and Chemistry.
facts.question: Who is the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences?

facts.title: The discovery of penicillin
facts.statement: Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928 after noticing mould killing bacteria on a contaminated culture plate he had left out.
facts.question: Who discovered penicillin?
facts.hook: An untidy laboratory produced the most important drug of the 20th century.

facts.title: Photo 51
facts.statement: Rosalind Franklin's X-ray diffraction image, Photo 51, provided the crucial evidence for the double-helix structure of DNA.
facts.question: Whose X-ray image, Photo 51, revealed the structure of DNA?

facts.title: The periodic table
facts.statement: Dmitri Mendeleev published the periodic table in 1869 and left gaps for elements not yet discovered — then correctly predicted their properties.
facts.question: Who created the periodic table of elements?
facts.hook: He predicted elements that had not been found yet, and was right.

facts.title: The Sun at the centre
facts.statement: Nicolaus Copernicus proposed that the Earth orbits the Sun, published in 1543, displacing the Earth-centred model.
facts.question: Who proposed that the Earth orbits the Sun?

facts.title: Laws of planetary motion
facts.statement: Johannes Kepler showed that planets move in ellipses, not circles, and derived three laws governing their orbits.
facts.question: Who discovered that planetary orbits are ellipses?

facts.title: The father of genetics
facts.statement: Gregor Mendel, a monk breeding pea plants, worked out the basic laws of inheritance in the 1860s — work ignored for 35 years.
facts.question: Who discovered the basic laws of inheritance using pea plants?

facts.title: Germ theory
facts.statement: Louis Pasteur established that microbes cause disease and spoilage, and gave his name to pasteurisation.
facts.question: Who established germ theory and gave his name to pasteurisation?

facts.title: Alternating current
facts.statement: Nikola Tesla developed the alternating-current system that won the 'war of the currents' and powers the world's electricity grids.
facts.question: Who developed the alternating-current electrical system?

facts.title: Black hole radiation
facts.statement: Stephen Hawking showed that black holes emit radiation and slowly evaporate — now called Hawking radiation.
facts.question: Who showed that black holes emit radiation and slowly evaporate?

facts.title: The first computer programmer
facts.statement: Ada Lovelace wrote what is considered the first algorithm intended for a machine, for Babbage's Analytical Engine in the 1840s.
facts.question: Who wrote the first published algorithm intended for a machine?
facts.hook: She saw that a calculating machine could manipulate symbols, not just numbers — a century early.
facts.details:
Augusta Ada King, Countess of Lovelace (née Byron; 10 December 1815 – 27 November 1852), also known as Ada Lovelace, was an English mathematician and writer chiefly known for work on Charles Babbage's proposed mechanical general-purpose computer, the analytical engine. She was the first to recognise the machine had applications beyond pure calculation. Lovelace is often considered the first computer programmer.
Lovelace was the only legitimate child of poet Lord Byron and reformer Anne Isabella Milbanke. Lord Byron separated from his wife a month after Ada was born, and died when she was eight. Although often ill in childhood, Lovelace pursued her studies assiduously. She married William King in 1835. King was a Baron, and was created Viscount Ockham and 1st Earl of Lovelace in 1838. The name Lovelace was chosen because Ada was descended from the extinct Baron Lovelaces. The title given to her husband thus made Ada the Countess of Lovelace.

facts.title: The first vaccine
facts.statement: Edward Jenner created the first vaccine in 1796, using cowpox to protect against smallpox — the only human disease ever eradicated.
facts.question: Who developed the first vaccine, against smallpox?
facts.hook: 'Vaccine' comes from vacca, Latin for cow.

facts.title: The largest organ
facts.statement: The skin is the body's largest organ, covering roughly two square metres in an adult and renewing itself about every four weeks.
facts.question: What is the largest organ of the human body?

facts.title: The largest internal organ
facts.statement: The liver is the largest internal organ, performs over 500 functions, and is the only human organ that can regenerate substantially.
facts.question: What is the largest internal organ in the human body?

facts.title: The smallest bone
facts.statement: The stapes, in the middle ear, is the smallest bone in the human body at about 3 mm.
facts.question: What is the smallest bone in the human body?
facts.hook: One of three tiny ear bones: hammer, anvil and stirrup.

facts.title: The longest bone
facts.statement: The femur, or thigh bone, is the longest and strongest bone in the human body.
facts.question: What is the longest bone in the human body?
facts.details:
The femur (; pl.: femurs or femora ), or thigh bone is the only bone in the thigh — the region of the lower limb between the hip and the knee. In many four-legged animals, the femur is the upper bone of the hindleg.
The top of the femur fits into a socket in the pelvis called the hip joint, and the bottom of the femur connects to the shinbone (tibia) and kneecap (patella) to form the knee. In humans the femur is the  largest and thickest bone in the body.


== Structure ==
The femur is the only bone in the upper leg and the longest bone in the human body. The two femurs converge medially toward the knees, where they articulate with the proximal ends of the tibiae. The angle at which the femora converge is an important factor in determining the femoral-tibial angle. In females, thicker pelvic bones cause the femora to converge more than in males.
In the condition genu valgum (knock knee), the femurs converge so much that the knees touch. The opposite condition, genu varum (bow-leggedness), occurs when the femurs diverge.

facts.title: Where insulin is made
facts.statement: The pancreas produces insulin, the hormone that lets cells absorb glucose from the blood.
facts.question: Which organ produces insulin?

facts.title: The blood filters
facts.statement: The kidneys filter about 180 litres of blood every day, returning almost all of it and excreting the rest as urine.
facts.question: Which pair of organs filters waste from the blood?

facts.title: The oxygen carrier
facts.statement: Haemoglobin is the iron-containing protein in red blood cells that binds oxygen and gives blood its red colour.
facts.question: Which protein in red blood cells carries oxygen?

facts.title: The body's control centre
facts.statement: The brain uses about 20% of the body's energy despite being only about 2% of its mass.
facts.question: Which organ uses roughly 20% of the body's energy?

facts.title: Bones in the adult body
facts.statement: An adult human has 206 bones. Babies are born with around 300, many of which fuse as they grow.
facts.question: How many bones are there in the adult human body?
facts.hook: You lose bones as you grow up, not gain them.

facts.title: Chambers of the heart
facts.statement: The human heart has four chambers: two atria that receive blood and two ventricles that pump it out.
facts.question: How many chambers does the human heart have?

facts.title: Planets in the Solar System
facts.statement: There are eight planets in the Solar System since Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006.
facts.question: How many planets are in the Solar System?

facts.title: Human chromosomes
facts.statement: Human cells normally contain 46 chromosomes, arranged in 23 pairs.
facts.question: How many chromosomes are in a typical human cell?

facts.title: Elements in the periodic table
facts.statement: The periodic table currently contains 118 confirmed elements, the heaviest of which exist only briefly in laboratories.
facts.question: How many elements are in the periodic table?

facts.title: The force that holds orbits
facts.statement: Gravity is the weakest of the four fundamental forces, yet it shapes the universe because it acts across unlimited distance and never cancels out.
facts.question: Which fundamental force keeps planets in orbit around the Sun?
facts.hook: The weakest force wins at large scales because it only ever attracts.

facts.title: The measure of disorder
facts.statement: Entropy measures disorder in a system. The second law of thermodynamics says total entropy always increases, which is why time has a direction.
facts.question: What is the physical measure of disorder in a system?

facts.title: Resistance to change in motion
facts.statement: Inertia is an object's resistance to any change in its motion — the essence of Newton's first law.
facts.question: What is an object's resistance to a change in its motion called?

facts.title: Why ships float
facts.statement: Buoyancy is the upward force on an object in a fluid, equal to the weight of fluid it displaces — Archimedes' principle.
facts.question: Which principle explains why a steel ship floats?

facts.title: Why a straw looks bent
facts.statement: Refraction is the bending of light as it passes between materials of different density, which makes a straw look broken in a glass of water.
facts.question: What is the bending of light as it passes between materials called?

facts.title: The cosmic speed limit
facts.statement: Nothing carrying information can travel faster than light in a vacuum, about 299,792 km per second — a fixed limit for every observer.
facts.question: What is the universal speed limit for anything carrying information?

facts.title: Splitting the nucleus
facts.statement: Nuclear fission splits a heavy nucleus into lighter ones, releasing energy — the process behind nuclear power stations and the first atomic bombs.
facts.question: What is the splitting of a heavy atomic nucleus called?
facts.hook: Fission splits, fusion joins — the Sun does the second one.

facts.title: Unit of force
facts.statement: The newton is the SI unit of force — the force needed to accelerate one kilogram at one metre per second squared.
facts.question: What is the SI unit of force?

facts.title: Unit of power
facts.statement: The watt is the SI unit of power, equal to one joule per second, named after steam-engine pioneer James Watt.
facts.question: What is the SI unit of power?

facts.title: Unit of frequency
facts.statement: The hertz is the SI unit of frequency, meaning one cycle per second.
facts.question: What is the SI unit of frequency?

facts.title: Unit of electrical resistance
facts.statement: The ohm is the SI unit of electrical resistance, symbolised by the Greek letter omega.
facts.question: What is the SI unit of electrical resistance?
facts.details:
The ohm (symbol: Ω, the uppercase Greek letter omega) is the unit of electrical resistance in the International System of Units (SI). It is named after German physicist Georg Ohm (1789–1854). Various empirically derived standard units for electrical resistance were developed in connection with early telegraphy practice, and the British Association for the Advancement of Science proposed a unit derived from existing units of mass, length and time, and of a convenient scale for practical work as early as 1861.
Following the 2019 revision of the SI, in which the ampere and the kilogram were redefined in terms of fundamental constants, the ohm is now also defined as an exact value in terms of these constants.


== Definition ==
The ohm is defined as an electrical resistance between two points of a conductor when a constant potential difference of one volt (V), applied to these points, produces in the conductor a current of one ampere (A), the conductor not being the seat of any electromotive force.

In many cases the resistance of a conductor is approximately constant within a certain range of voltages, temperatures, and other parameters. These are called linear resistors. In other cases resistance varies, such as in the case of the thermistor, which exhibits a strong dependence of its resistance with temperature.

In the US, consecutive vowels in the prefixed units "kiloohm" and "megaohm" are commonly reduced to one, producing "kilohm" and "megohm".
In alternating current circuits, electrical impedance is also measured in ohms.

facts.title: Unit of energy
facts.statement: The joule is the SI unit of energy — roughly the energy needed to lift a small apple one metre.
facts.question: What is the SI unit of energy?

facts.title: Unit of pressure
facts.statement: The pascal is the SI unit of pressure, equal to one newton per square metre.
facts.question: What is the SI unit of pressure?

facts.title: The largest animal ever
facts.statement: The blue whale is the largest animal known to have existed, reaching 30 metres and 150 tonnes — its heart alone weighs as much as a small car.
facts.question: What is the largest animal that has ever lived?

facts.title: Fastest land animal
facts.statement: The cheetah is the fastest land animal, reaching about 110 km/h in short bursts.
facts.question: What is the fastest land animal?

facts.title: Fastest animal of all
facts.statement: The peregrine falcon is the fastest animal on Earth, exceeding 320 km/h in its hunting dive.
facts.question: What is the fastest animal in the world?
facts.hook: The cheetah wins on land; the falcon wins outright.

facts.title: Largest land animal
facts.statement: The African bush elephant is the largest living land animal, weighing up to about 6 tonnes.
facts.question: What is the largest land animal alive today?

facts.title: The only flying mammal
facts.statement: Bats are the only mammals capable of true sustained flight; flying squirrels merely glide.
facts.question: Which is the only mammal capable of true sustained flight?

facts.title: Three hearts and blue blood
facts.statement: An octopus has three hearts and blue blood, because it uses copper-based haemocyanin rather than iron-based haemoglobin.
facts.question: Which animal has three hearts and blue blood?

facts.title: The tallest animal
facts.statement: The giraffe is the tallest living animal, up to about 5.5 m, yet has the same number of neck vertebrae as a human: seven.
facts.question: What is the tallest living animal?
facts.hook: Seven neck bones — the same as yours, just much longer.

facts.title: The largest reptile
facts.statement: The saltwater crocodile is the largest living reptile, reaching over 6 metres, and has the strongest measured bite of any animal.
facts.question: What is the largest living reptile?

facts.title: The particle with positive charge
facts.statement: Protons carry a positive charge and sit in the nucleus. The number of protons defines which element an atom is.
facts.question: Which subatomic particle carries a positive charge?

facts.title: The particle of light
facts.statement: The photon is the quantum of light — massless, always travelling at light speed, and carrying the electromagnetic force.
facts.question: What is the particle of light called?

facts.title: The negatively charged particle
facts.statement: Electrons carry a negative charge and orbit the nucleus. Their movement is what we call electricity.
facts.question: Which subatomic particle carries a negative charge?

facts.title: What protons are made of
facts.statement: Quarks are the fundamental particles that combine in threes to form protons and neutrons. They are never found alone.
facts.question: Which fundamental particles combine to form protons and neutrons?

facts.title: The ghost particle
facts.statement: Neutrinos barely interact with matter — trillions pass through your body every second — which is why they are nicknamed ghost particles.
facts.question: Which nearly massless particle passes through matter almost without interacting?

facts.title: The formula H2O
facts.statement: Water is H2O — two hydrogen atoms bonded to one oxygen. Its unusual property of expanding when it freezes is why ice floats.
facts.question: Which compound has the chemical formula H2O?
facts.hook: Almost everything contracts when it freezes; water does the opposite, which is why lakes freeze from the top.

facts.title: The formula NaCl
facts.statement: Sodium chloride, common table salt, is formed from a violently reactive metal and a poisonous gas.
facts.question: What is the chemical name for common table salt, NaCl?

facts.title: The formula CO2
facts.statement: Carbon dioxide is what animals exhale and plants absorb, and the principal greenhouse gas driving climate change.
facts.question: Which gas has the chemical formula CO2?

facts.title: The formula CH4
facts.statement: Methane is the main component of natural gas and a greenhouse gas far more potent than CO2 over the short term.
facts.question: Which gas has the chemical formula CH4?

facts.title: The formula NH3
facts.statement: Ammonia, NH3, is central to fertiliser production; the Haber process that makes it feeds roughly half the world's population.
facts.question: Which compound has the chemical formula NH3?

facts.title: The molecule of heredity
facts.statement: DNA carries genetic instructions in a double helix, with the bases adenine, thymine, cytosine and guanine pairing across the strands.
facts.question: Which molecule carries genetic instructions in a double helix?

facts.title: The study of earthquakes
facts.statement: Seismology is the study of earthquakes and the propagation of elastic waves through the Earth.
facts.question: What is the study of earthquakes called?

facts.title: The study of birds
facts.statement: Ornithology is the branch of zoology devoted to birds.
facts.question: What is the study of birds called?

facts.title: The study of fossils
facts.statement: Palaeontology is the study of ancient life through fossils, spanning everything from microbes to dinosaurs.
facts.question: What is the study of fossils called?

facts.title: The study of fungi
facts.statement: Mycology is the study of fungi — a kingdom more closely related to animals than to plants.
facts.question: What is the study of fungi called?
facts.hook: Fungi are genetically closer to you than to a tree.

facts.title: The study of weather
facts.statement: Meteorology is the science of the atmosphere and weather forecasting.
facts.question: What is the scientific study of weather called?

facts.title: The mosquito-borne parasite
facts.statement: Malaria is caused by Plasmodium parasites transmitted by female Anopheles mosquitoes, and still kills hundreds of thousands of people a year.
facts.question: Which disease is caused by a parasite spread by Anopheles mosquitoes?

facts.title: The sailors' disease
facts.statement: Scurvy is caused by vitamin C deficiency and devastated long sea voyages until citrus rations were introduced.
facts.question: Which disease is caused by a deficiency of vitamin C?

facts.title: The Black Death
facts.statement: The bubonic plague, caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, killed perhaps a third of Europe's population in the 1340s.
facts.question: Which disease caused the Black Death of the 1340s?

facts.title: The vitamin D deficiency
facts.statement: Rickets softens and weakens children's bones and is caused by a lack of vitamin D, calcium or phosphate.
facts.question: Which childhood bone disease is caused by vitamin D deficiency?

facts.title: How plants make food
facts.statement: Photosynthesis converts light, water and carbon dioxide into sugars and oxygen — the process that put oxygen into Earth's atmosphere.
facts.question: What is the process by which plants convert light into chemical energy?

facts.title: The powerhouse of the cell
facts.statement: Mitochondria generate most of a cell's energy and carry their own DNA, a remnant of the bacteria they descend from.
facts.question: Which cell structure generates most of the cell's energy?
facts.hook: They were once free-living bacteria, and still keep their own genome.
